implementation_notes: The Kotlin standard library already is a combinator toolkit: `Result` carries `map`/`flatMap`/`fold`/`getOrElse`, `Sequence` provides lazy `map`/`filter`/`fold` chains documented as intermediate and terminal operations, and the scoping functions (`let`, `run`, `also`, `apply`, `takeIf`) compose ordinary values without any class. A domain DSL is usually a few extension functions and infix combinators over a small sealed type, which retires hand-written Strategy/Command hierarchies; keep the classic structure when the DSL must be introspectable or shipped as a stable public API, where a sealed interface plus documented combinators is more honest than a bag of extension functions.
pitfalls: `Result` is not a general-purpose monad: it cannot be used as a return type through every signature, and its failure state assumes exceptions, so a non-exception domain error fits `Either` better.
Sequences are lazy but re-iterated per terminal call: a stored sequence re-runs its side effects, and single-use sequences (from an iterator) throw on the second pass.
Extension/infix combinators resolve statically: when inference falls back to `Any`, the wrong overload compiles and the mistake appears at runtime.

variants.name: Arrow: Either/Validated with the Raise DSL
variants.implementation_notes: Arrow generalises the pattern to typed errors: `Either<A, B>` (and `Ior`, `Validated`) with `map`/`flatMap`/`fold`/`getOrElse`, plus the `Raise<E>` computation context (`either { }`, `ensure`, `bind`, `recover`) so failures are values in the signature rather than exceptions. Its accumulating combinators (`zipOrAccumulate`, `mapOrAccumulate`, `sequence`) express 'all of these must succeed, collect every error' - the part the standard library's `Result` cannot do. Choose Arrow when typed, accumulated failures dominate the domain; keep the stdlib variant when exceptions and `Result` suffice.
pitfalls: The `Raise` context and `kotlin.Result` are different worlds: mixing them requires explicit conversions and erases the typed error the DSL was built to carry.
Accumulation only happens through the accruing combinators - calling `flatMap`/`bind` short-circuits on the first failure, so 'collect all errors' silently degenerates.
The DSL hides control flow: `raise`/`bind` look like ordinary calls, so readers must know the enclosing scope to see that a function can fail.
